projects.name: AgentMate CRM Mobile
projects.summary: A ~92,000-line Flutter client I created and authored — 182 of 189 Dart files, 20 Provider modules. Offline business-card capture on Hive, conversation transcription with AI-extracted action items, and spoken appointment reminders written in native Kotlin and Swift.
projects.lead: The Flutter client for a multi-tenant real-estate CRM. I created the repository and wrote 182 of its 189 Dart files.

sections.heading: Overview
body: About 92,000 lines organised as one Provider module per feature — contacts, deals, tasks, calendar, expenses, banking, conversations and chat — all scoped to a selected workspace. Every module talks to a workspace-prefixed REST API through a single HTTP client handling tokens, timeouts and multipart uploads.

sections.heading: The business problem
body: Agents work from their phones between showings. A CRM that only works at a desk collects nothing: business cards go uncaptured, conversations go unlogged, and follow-ups are missed. The app had to keep working with no signal and reconcile cleanly when it returned.

sections.heading: What I built
list: Google sign-in plus a server-auth-code flow so the backend can hold a refresh token for Contacts and Calendar, with disconnect and reconnect handled through record parking.
An offline business-card queue on Hive with retry counts, syncing when connectivity returns.
Conversation capture: AAC recording, upload, transcription polling, and playback with a synced transcript and editable AI-extracted action items.

Spoken appointment reminders in native code — Kotlin exact alarms with a text-to-speech foreground service and boot receiver, Swift notification triggers and speech synthesis — over one shared MethodChannel contract.
A documented 20-bug hardening sweep and around ten signed releases with R8 minification.

sections.heading: Architecture
body: Provider / ChangeNotifier at scale: 20 feature modules with workspace-scoped cache clearing and disposed-notifier guards, singleton services exposing broadcast streams, and a single HTTP client with central 401 handling.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: Google Contacts and Calendar need server-side refresh tokens, not the mobile access token — solved with a server-auth-code exchange.
Offline capture must not duplicate on resync — retry-counted Hive queue entries with server-side reconciliation.
Native reminders had to behave identically on both platforms — one channel contract, two implementations, payloads passed through shared preferences.

outcomes: Primary author: 224 of 286 commits and 182 of 189 Dart files.
20 feature modules in production use.
Around ten signed releases with R8 minification and a documented 20-bug hardening sweep.

projects.name: EnServicePortal
projects.summary: Site staff record build defects in concrete shells with no network. I wrote almost all of it, including a 2,127-line PouchDB layer that stores everything locally and syncs on reconnect, and fabric.js annotation over floor plans. One codebase ships to Android, iOS and web.
projects.lead: An offline-first Angular, Ionic and Capacitor application used on construction sites. I wrote 170 of its 179 commits.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Site staff open a suite, mark deficiencies on floor-plan layouts and photographs, annotate the photographs, run checklist inspections, record colour selections and suite customisations, watch construction status and generate reports — all of it working offline and syncing when connectivity returns.

sections.heading: The business problem
body: Deficiency walk-throughs happen in concrete shells with no Wi-Fi and unreliable mobile data, and the output — what is wrong, where, with photographic proof, assigned to which trade — is the legal and financial record for handover. Paper lists and camera rolls lose location context and cannot be reconciled afterwards.

sections.heading: The solution
body: Local-first storage, not a sync afterthought. A 2,127-line PouchDB layer holds projects, suites, deficiencies, checklists and media as local documents; every write lands locally first and reconciles on reconnect, so a walk-through completes with no signal and nothing is lost if the app is killed.

sections.heading: What I built
list: The offline data layer — the PouchDB service, its document model and the reconnect sync.
Deficiency capture and resolution across three screens totalling ~8,600 lines: create, categorise, locate, assign, comment on and close defects, with per-suite and per-project rollups.
Photo and floor-plan annotation on a fabric.js canvas, with pinned locations editable after the fact.
Checklist inspections — templated runs with pass/fail items, notes, photographs and signature capture.
Construction dashboards, charted reports with CSV export, a PDF document viewer and change history.
Native packaging: Capacitor camera, filesystem, network-state and voice recording across Android and iOS.

sections.heading: Architecture
body: Angular with Ionic components and Capacitor for native packaging. Pages under one feature folder, and three services: a REST client, a shared cross-page state service, and the PouchDB offline layer that is the heart of the application.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: No connectivity on site — PouchDB local-first writes with reconnect sync, the pattern I later carried into Flutter with Hive and SQLite.
Defects need a location, not just a description — canvas annotation over floor plans with editable pins.
Very large screens: the largest page reached 3,410 lines under delivery pressure. The honest answer is that I would split it by concern and move state out of the page.
One codebase, two stores and the web — Ionic components with Capacitor native plugins over a single Angular application.

outcomes: 170 of 179 commits over two years of continuous delivery.
~22,300 lines of TypeScript across 24 page modules.
Offline capability, plus Android, iOS and web builds from one codebase.

projects.name: ATM-CRM
projects.summary: Contacts, deals and commissions, Gmail inbox, calendar and tasks, expenses and banking. I worked both sides and owned the integrations: Google OAuth with two-way Calendar and Tasks sync, OpenAI extraction from receipts and bank statements, and fuzzy transaction matching.
projects.lead: A workspace-scoped CRM for real-estate agents, built as a monorepo: Vue 3 client, Express and MongoDB server.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Contacts, deals and commissions, a Gmail inbox, calendar and tasks, expenses, banking, documents, mileage, newsletters and AI assistance — every record scoped to a workspace, with role-based access throughout.

sections.heading: The business problem
body: Agents run their business across a mailbox, a calendar, a spreadsheet of commissions and a shoebox of receipts. The value is not another database — it is pulling those sources together without the agent re-typing anything, and without the sync silently corrupting their calendar.

sections.heading: What I built
list: Google OAuth 2.0 code flow with per-workspace token storage, refresh handling and incremental scopes.
Two-way Calendar and Tasks sync with conflict-safe upserts, and disconnect/reconnect record parking so nothing is orphaned.

OpenAI-powered extraction: JSON-mode structured output from emails, vision OCR for receipts and business cards, and PDF bank statements parsed through the Files API — each with duplicate detection and user confirmation before any record is written.
Fuzzy matching of imported bank transactions against recorded expenses.
Server-side pagination, filter and sort contracts shared across modules.

sections.heading: Architecture
body: A monorepo with a Vite-built Vue 3 client and an Express server on MongoDB. Workspace-prefixed routes, merged-param nested routers, a consistent response envelope, and two-layer JWT sessions with revocation.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: Calendar sync that cannot duplicate or delete a user's events — conflict-safe upserts keyed on external identifiers, with parking for records whose link is broken.
LLM output is not trustworthy by default — JSON mode, schema validation, duplicate detection and an explicit confirmation step before writing.
Long-running AI requests must be cancellable — AbortController threaded end to end.

outcomes: 379 of 616 commits — primary author across client and server.
Google Workspace, OpenAI and banking integrations in production use.
Documented architecture and sync design carried into sibling services.

projects.name: HomeFoody
projects.summary: A home-food marketplace for an Australian client, Cybertree. I was the only mobile developer on both apps: supplier onboarding, a date-and-time-slot availability calendar, menus and promotions; and on the buyer side, OTP sign-in, discovery and a cart grouped by supplier.

media.alt: HomeFoody supplier app dashboard showing availability toggle, order totals and recent orders

projects.lead: Two Flutter apps published to Google Play and the App Store, plus the Vue 3 admin console behind them. I was the only mobile developer on both.

sections.heading: Overview
body: HomeFoody connects home cooks with buyers nearby. The supplier app lets a cook run their kitchen as a small business — register through a multi-step onboarding flow, publish menu items with photos, declare exactly which dates and time slots they can cook, run promotional campaigns and manage orders. The customer app handles discovery, ordering and tracking.

sections.heading: The business problem
body: A home cook is not a restaurant. They cook on some days and not others, in limited quantities, within windows that change week to week. Marketplace software built for restaurants assumes continuous opening hours and stock. On the buyer side, one basket can hold dishes from several independent cooks with different pickup windows — a checkout that discovers this at the end fails the order.

sections.heading: The solution
body: Availability became a first-class concept rather than an afterthought: a dedicated provider derives month and week views, per-date time slots and default weekday patterns, with a modal editor that reconciles bulk changes back into the page. On the buyer side the cart groups items by supplier all the way through checkout and order history, so per-cook totals and constraints are visible from the start.

sections.heading: What I built
list: Supplier onboarding — a stepped flow with cascading country → state → suburb → postcode selection, a searchable suburb modal and per-field validation.
The availability calendar — month and week views over a ~976-line provider deriving selectable time blocks.
Menu and promotions — an item editor with MIME-typed multipart image upload, plus campaigns with promo codes, discount types, minimum order and banner artwork.
Order management — the supplier order screen with pickup and delivery context, items, totals and status transitions.
Customer discovery and cart — OTP sign-in, geolocation with a manual city fallback, persisted cuisine filters and sorting, and the supplier-grouped cart through to checkout.

Store readiness — Firebase Cloud Messaging with local-notification presentation, connectivity handling, account deletion for store policy, icons and splash screens, and fifteen releases across the two apps.

sections.heading: Architecture
body: Provider / ChangeNotifier state, pages organised by feature, typed models, and a single HTTP layer handling tokens from secure storage, timeouts, multipart upload and logout. The Node/Express/MongoDB backend was a colleague's work; the Vue 3 admin console — suppliers, customers, orders, promotions, admins and an activity audit — is mine, sole-authored.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: Availability is not opening hours — solved with a dedicated provider rather than a calendar widget, so the supplier's own selections drive what buyers can order.
Non-technical users on small screens — one decision per screen, searchable geography pickers, inline error text next to the field that caused it.
Patchy mobile connectivity — connectivity checks with a dedicated no-internet screen, and one HTTP layer handling timeouts and unauthenticated responses uniformly.
Two store review processes — account deletion, permission usage strings and consent checkboxes added before submission. Both apps passed.

projects.name: AgentMate Public Website
projects.scale: One app serving every tenant site
projects.summary: One Nuxt 3 application server-renders every agent and brokerage site on the platform, resolving the tenant from the host header in Nitro middleware and building pages from API-driven section config. My work concentrated on SSR correctness: context across awaits, hydration, first paint.
projects.lead: A multi-tenant Nuxt 3 renderer: one application serves every agent and brokerage website on the platform.

sections.heading: Overview
body: The tenant is resolved from the host header in Nitro middleware, then each page is composed from API-driven page and section configuration, with an in-browser editor mode for the people who own the content. Per-tenant branding is delivered through CSS variables, so one build serves every tenant without a per-tenant deploy.

sections.heading: The business problem
body: Every agent wants their own site, and no platform can afford to build or deploy one per agent. The alternative — a single rendering engine driven by configuration — only works if server rendering is correct, because these are public, SEO-critical pages.

sections.heading: What I built
list: Section rendering from API-driven configuration, with the editor mode that writes it back.
SSR correctness work: Nuxt context propagation across awaits, hydration determinism, and eliminating unstyled first paint.
Per-tenant theming through CSS custom properties rather than per-tenant builds.
Server routes for sitemap and robots generation per tenant.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: Losing the Nuxt context after an await inside middleware — resolved with explicit context propagation.
Hydration mismatches caused by tenant-dependent rendering — made deterministic by resolving the tenant before render rather than during it.
One build, many brands — CSS variables set at the document level per tenant.

outcomes: 703 of 1,485 commits — one of two principal contributors.
A single application rendering every tenant site in production.

projects.name: ATM Mileage Tracker
projects.summary: Offline-first SQLite sync queue with idempotency keys and backoff, Ramer–Douglas–Peucker path simplification, and a duplicate-trip bug caused by the plugin running a second isolate.
projects.lead: Automatic background trip capture for mileage reimbursement, synced to the CRM at a per-kilometre rate.

sections.heading: Overview
body: The app records driving trips without the user starting anything, filters GPS noise, simplifies the path, and syncs each trip to the CRM. A teammate built the first tracking engine; I joined after v1 and own about 70% of the commits.

sections.heading: What I built
list: Backend integration — login via Google token exchange, workspace selection, a REST client with timeouts and 401 handling.
An offline-first SQLite sync queue with client-generated UUIDs as idempotency keys, exponential backoff and a visible failed state.
Ramer–Douglas–Peucker path simplification at an 8-metre epsilon, plus accuracy gates, implausible-speed rejection and centroid-based stationary detection.
The native iOS side in Swift — CoreMotion activity recognition and a CLLocationManager keep-alive — and the Podfile permission macros.
Test tooling: GPX routes and ADB scripts for the emulator, a 48-finding QA audit and a 21-case device plan.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: Duplicate trips after reboot: the foreground-task plugin runs a second isolate, so the singleton location service existed twice. Fixed with an owner/companion model keyed on which isolate started the service.
Battery versus accuracy — adaptive location settings driven by movement state.
At-least-once delivery without duplicate trips server-side — client UUID idempotency keys.

outcomes: 68 of 97 commits after joining a running project.
RDP simplification materially reduces the stored and transmitted path.
A 48-finding QA audit and a 21-case device test plan, both authored by me.

Multi-currency pricing without drift between catalogue, quotation and order.

Admissions, events, discounts and promo codes, and orders.

Portal CMS and settings for non-technical content owners.

projects.name: SettlementFormPOC
projects.summary: A funder-agnostic intake engine where everything is data, not code: a json-logic engine interprets form definitions held in MongoDB — computed scoring, skip logic, inference, thresholds and render plan.
projects.lead: A proof of concept for settlement-services intake, written end to end by me in a TypeScript monorepo.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Form definitions live in MongoDB and are interpreted at runtime by an isomorphic engine package shared by client and server: computed scoring, skip logic, inference, thresholds, a render plan and multilingual resolution. Adding a new funder's form means adding data, not code.

sections.heading: What I built
body: Everything — the engine package, the React client, the Express API, the schema and the tests. 14 of 14 commits.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: Keeping one engine correct on both sides of the wire — an isomorphic package consumed by client and server alike.
Expressing scoring and skip logic as data without inventing a new language — json-logic as the interpreter.

outcomes: Sole author: 14 of 14 commits.
The only project in my portfolio that is safely publishable as source — a POC over a public government form, with no employer data in it.
projects.noAssetsNote: It is a proof of concept rather than a released product, and no interface captures were kept. It is also the one project here whose source could be published, since it is sole-authored and built over a public government form with no employer data in it.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Part of a nine-service backend. I built the podcast and episode APIs, a monologue service, and AI voice generation across multiple providers, with credit metering that charges per model at its own price.

sections.heading: What I built
list: Podcast and episode APIs.
The monologue service.
Multi-provider AI voice generation with provider fallback.
Credit metering and per-model price charging.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
list: Paid generation must never run without metering — credits are reserved before the provider call and reconciled after it.
Providers price differently per model, so charging had to be model-aware rather than per-request.

outcomes: 14 of 285 commits — a focused contribution, not ownership of the platform.
First production AI work, a year before the OpenAI features in the CRM.
